_comment: The source catalogue (committed). One entry per stream: its page at /<slug> and its listener. listed=false keeps a source off the landing page (reachable by URL, noindex). listener.input is a URL or a file on the server; local_input overrides it for scripts/dev.sh. Ports must be unique. rights records the basis for analysing and relaying the audio (audio=true).

sources.name: Sonic Division
sources.subtitle: Live listening
meta: Silos on the dry lake bed
sources.summary: Satellite Radio from the Silos at Owens Dry Lake. Metabolic Studio's Sonic Division transmits a live feed of the sounds produced by the Silos and the environment around the dry lake bed in Payahuunadu (the Owens Valley); on occasion you will hear in-situ performances from within the Silos.

credit.note: Satellite Radio from the Silos at Owens Dry Lake (Payahuunadu)

sources.rights: Metabolic Studio. No licence stated. Live listening is offered publicly; permission for the analysis and the in-browser audio relay was requested on 2026-10-01 and is pending.

sources.name: VLF Natural Radio · Heidelberg
sources.subtitle: Live listening
meta: Very low frequency radio, up to 16 kHz
sources.summary: Earth's own radio. A receiver near Heidelberg turns very low frequency radio waves into sound: the crackle of lightning strikes thousands of kilometres away (sferics), falling tones that travel along the magnetic field (whistlers), and the steady hum of the power grid.
sources.rights: Stefan Schäfer (dk7fc.info) agreed to the use on 2026-10-01.

sources.name: VLF Natural Radio · Cumiana
sources.subtitle: Live listening
meta: Very low frequency radio, up to 16 kHz
sources.summary: Earth's own radio from the foot of the western Alps. Renato Romero's receiver in Cumiana, near Turin, turns very low frequency radio waves into sound: the crackle of distant lightning (sferics), falling tones that travel along the magnetic field (whistlers), and the hum of the power grid.
sources.rights: Renato Romero (vlf.it); relayed by dk7fc.info, whose operator agreed on 2026-10-01. No licence stated; permission from Renato Romero requested 2026-10-01, pending.

sources.name: VLF Natural Radio · Heathcote
sources.subtitle: Live listening
meta: Very low frequency radio, up to 16 kHz
sources.summary: Earth's own radio from the southern hemisphere. The receiver at the Leon Mow Radio Observatory, a dark-sky site of the Astronomical Society of Victoria near Heathcote, turns very low frequency radio waves into sound: the crackle of distant lightning (sferics), whistlers along the magnetic field, and the hum of the power grid.

sources.rights: Leon Mow Radio Observatory (asv.org.au). No licence stated; relayed by dk7fc.info, whose operator agreed on 2026-10-01. Permission from the receiver's operator requested 2026-10-01, pending.

sources.name: Mars · InSight
sources.subtitle: Archive listening
meta: Seismometer: wind, marsquakes, the lander itself
sources.summary: Sound from the surface of Mars, heard through a seismometer. NASA's InSight lander felt the Martian wind, two marsquakes and the ticking of its own parts cooling at night; these recordings, sped up or raised in pitch to become audible, play here in a 21-minute loop.

credit.note: archive recordings from NASA's Sounds from Beyond

sources.rights: NASA media usage guidelines: free to use with credit (NASA/JPL-Caltech/CNES/IPGP), no implied endorsement. Clips listed in docs/sources.md.

sources.name: Jupiter · Juno
sources.subtitle: Archive listening
meta: Jupiter and its moons Ganymede and Europa
Radio and plasma waves, shifted into hearing range
sources.summary: Jupiter's radio voice. The Waves instrument on NASA's Juno spacecraft records radio and plasma waves around the planet; shifted into the range of hearing they become rising tones, whoops and crackle. A 4-minute loop from the flybys of Ganymede and Europa and from Jupiter itself.

credit.note: archive recordings; University of Iowa clips licensed CC BY 3.0

sources.rights: NASA media usage guidelines (Ganymede flyby clip) and University of Iowa clips under CC BY 3.0 (NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/University of Iowa). Clips listed in docs/sources.md.

sources.name: Amsterdam · Hydrophile 1
sources.subtitle: Live listening
sources.summary: Under the surface of Amsterdam's water. A hydrophone streams live what the city's water carries: boats and engines, currents, and the life below the waterline. Streamed by sound artist Lia Mazzari with a streambox, one of the small open-microphone transmitters of Soundcamp and Acoustic Commons that share live environmental sound through the Locus Sonus stream server.
sources.rights: Lia Mazzari / Soundcamp. No licence stated. Live listening is offered publicly; permission for the analysis and the in-browser audio relay was requested on 2026-10-01 and is pending.

sources.name: Svalbard · Bayelva
sources.subtitle: Live listening
sources.summary: A permanent microphone at the Bayelva long-term observation site near Ny-Ålesund, where the Alfred Wegener Institute has monitored the climate and the frozen ground since 1998. Since July 2025 it lets the Arctic be heard as it changes: wind, meltwater, weather and the rare passing visitor. Part of Common Grounds, a collaboration between sonic practice and climate science.

credit.text: Common Grounds (Julia Boike, AWI; Kerstin Ergenzinger; Bnaya Halperin-Kaddari) — radio.earth

sources.rights: radio.earth / Common Grounds. No licence stated. Live listening is offered publicly; permission for the analysis and the in-browser audio relay was requested on 2026-10-01 and is pending.

sources.name: Brno · Park Lužánky
sources.subtitle: Live listening
sources.summary: A microphone in Lužánky, the largest park in Brno and the oldest public park in the Czech Republic. Restored meadows, a brook and old trees drew 72 species of birds in a 2016 count, so dawn and dusk choruses overlap with footsteps, voices and the hum of the city. Listening continuously since spring 2021.

credit.text: Tomáš Šenkyrík, Vit Kalvoda, Udo Noll — radio.earth

sources.rights: radio.earth. No licence stated. Live listening is offered publicly; permission for the analysis and the in-browser audio relay was requested on 2026-10-01 and is pending.

sources.name: Kozmice · Bird Meadows
sources.subtitle: Live listening
meta: Floodplain meadows of the Opava River
sources.summary: A solar-powered listening station in the Kozmice meadows, one of the last floodplain areas of the Opava River. The long-term project listens to how the soundscape of the river and its living floodplain changes: birds, insects, wind and water, through the seasons.
